name: Architectural photography
summary: Photographs of buildings with upright lines, clean light and a chosen hour. The picture shows the form, the material and the way a building sits in its place.

philosophy.core_thesis: A building is judged in a picture, so the picture must keep its lines true and choose the light that shows its form.
design_principles: Use a tilt-shift lens of 24mm to 45mm, or a view camera, and keep the camera back parallel to the facade, so that verticals stay at 0°.
Stop down to f/11 to f/16 at ISO 100, on a tripod, with a shutter of 1/15s to 2s.
Choose the hour: low sun at 15° to 30° for a facade, or blue hour with interior lamps lit for a glow.
Shoot at 1.5m height for a plan view of the facade, or raise to 3m to 6m for a clean top line.
Keep people small or absent; use a figure at 1/20 of the frame height for scale.
Grade to neutral colour: keep the true tone of the material, and keep shadow detail.
anti_patterns: Converging verticals from a tilted camera
Flat grey light with no shadow modelling
Cars and signs that block the form
Colour casts that change the material

composition.framing: Complete and level; the building sits whole or in a bold crop with true verticals.
composition.viewpoint: Level at 1.5m to 3m, 10m to 60m from the facade; the camera is square or at a 30° to 45° corner view.
composition.geometry: Verticals, horizontals and receding diagonals; the grid of the facade sets the rhythm.
composition.subject_placement: Centred for a frontal view, or on a third for a corner view; sky takes 15–30%.

principles.rule: Place the axis of a frontal facade at 0.5 of the width, within 0.02.
Use 2 to 4 receding lines from a wall or a path that meet at one vanishing point.
Repeat the bay or the window at a constant pitch, with 6 to 30 repeats across the frame.
Leave 15–30% of the frame as sky and 10–20% as ground.
Keep the 4:5 or 3:2 frame and a facade that fills 70–85% of the height.

light.quality: Clear and directional for form; soft and even for a dusk glow.
light.direction: Low sun from the side at 15° to 30° elevation; at blue hour, interior lamps at 3000K against a sky at 7000K.
light.key_to_fill_ratio: 3:1 to 4:1 on a facade; 1:1 at blue hour
light.time_of_day: One to two hours after sunrise, one hour before sunset, or blue hour

lens_and_camera.format: View camera 4×5 in, or digital full frame or medium format with tilt-shift
lens_and_camera.focus: Focus one third into the scene; the depth of field covers 10m to infinity.
lens_and_camera.support: Heavy tripod with a geared head and a spirit level

colour_and_grade.treatment: Neutral colour with true material tone and open shadows; a quiet blue sky.
grade_recipe: Set the white balance at 5500K, tint 0.
Set the black point at 2% and the white point at 97%.
Lift shadows by +20 and lower highlights by −15.
Correct verticals and horizontals to 0° and keep the original crop at 95% or more.
Lower saturation by −5% and keep the material hue true.
Blend 2 or 3 exposures by hand for the windows; no automatic HDR.

subject_and_staging.staging: Prepared: clear cars and bins, switch on interior lights, and wait for a clear sky and the hour.
subject_and_staging.direction: Place a single person at 1/20 of the frame height on a route line for scale.

workflow: Shoot a bracket of 3 to 5 frames at ±1 stop.
Blend windows and sky by hand.
Correct perspective to 0° and clean up distractions.
Export at 4:5 and 3:2, sRGB, 3000px on the long edge.
post_processing.output: A true-line, evenly graded building image for a magazine, a monograph or a practice site.

positive: low golden sun on the facade

emotion.target_response: Calm admiration: the viewer sees the order and the light of a place and wants to be there.

use_cases: image prompts for true-line building views
avoid_when: The brief needs candid street life around the building.
The only lens is a wide-angle phone camera with no correction.

modifiers.how: Use flat overcast light at 1.5:1, a frontal level view and a series of 20 or more of one building type; print large.
Go inside with window light at 2:1, a 24mm tilt-shift at f/8 and 3 to 5 styled objects; keep the verticals at 0°.

focal_length.note: A tilt-shift lens of 17 to 45 mm, or 90 to 135 mm on 4×5 in, gives this band.

sources.title: Julius Shulman, Photographing Architecture and Interiors (Whitney Library of Design, 1962)
Ezra Stoller, The Seagram Building (Princeton Architectural Press, 1999)
